questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The velocity $v$ of a particle depends on time $t$ as $v = at^2 + \frac{\beta}{t+\gamma}$. The dimension of $\alpha\beta/\gamma$ is:
questions.solution:
Using the principle of homogeneity:
- In the term $(\gamma + t)$, dimensions of $\gamma$ must be equal to dimensions of $t$. So, $[\gamma] = [T]$.
- The term $\alpha t^2$ must have dimensions of velocity. $[\alpha] \, [T^2] = [LT^{-1}] \implies [\alpha] = [LT^{-3}]$.
- The term $\frac{\beta}{t+\gamma}$ must have dimensions of velocity. $\frac{[\beta]}{[T]} = [LT^{-1}] \implies [\beta] = [L]$.
The dimensions of the expression $\alpha\beta/\gamma$ are:
$$\left[\frac{\alpha\beta}{\gamma}\right] = \frac{[LT^{-3}][L]}{[T]} = [L^2T^{-4}]$$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The equation of state for a real gas is given by $(P + \frac{a}{V^2}) (V - b) = RT$. The dimensions of the quantity $ab/R$ are:
questions.solution:
From the principle of homogeneity:
- The term $\frac{a}{V^2}$ has dimensions of pressure $P$. $[a] = [P][V^2] = [ML^{-1}T^{-2}] \, [L^6] = [ML^5T^{-2}]$.
- The term $b$ has dimensions of volume $V$. $[b] = [L^3]$.
- The term $RT$ has dimensions of energy ($PV$). So, $[R][K] = [ML^2T^{-2}]$, which gives $[R] = [ML^2T^{-2}K^{-1}]$.

The dimensions of the required quantity are:
$$\left[\frac{ab}{R}\right] = \frac{[ML^5T^{-2}][L^3]}{[ML^2T^{-2}K^{-1}]} = \frac{[ML^8T^{-2}]}{[ML^2T^{-2}K^{-1}]} = [L^6K]$$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The physical quantity having dimensions $[M^{-1}L^{-3}T^3 A^2]$ is:
questions.solution:
We determine the dimensions for each of the given options.
- Resistance $(R)$ : $[R] = [ML^2T^{-3}A^{-2}]$.
- Permittivity $(\epsilon_0)$ : From Coulomb's Law, $F = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}$. $[\epsilon_0] = \frac{[q]^2}{[F][r]^2} = \frac{[AT]^2}{[MLT^{-2}][L]^2} = [M^{-1}L^{-3}T^4A^2]$.
- Resistivity $(\rho)$ : From $R = \rho \frac{l}{A}$, $[\rho] = \frac{[R][A]}{[l]} = \frac{[ML^2T^{-3}A^{-2}][L^2]}{[L]} = [ML^3T^{-3}A^{-2}]$. Electrical Conductivity $(\sigma)$ is the reciprocal of resistivity, so $[\sigma] = \frac{1}{[\rho]} = [M^{-1}L^{-3}T^3A^2]$.
- Permeability $(\mu_0)$ : From $F = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \frac{I_1 I_2 l}{r}$, $[\mu_0] = \frac{[F][r]}{[I]^2[l]} = \frac{[MLT^{-2}][L]}{[A^2][L]} = [MLT^{-2}A^{-2}]$.
The given dimension $[M^{-1}L^{-3}T^3A^2]$ matches that of Electrical Conductivity.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A quantity $\eta = \frac{\phi_E}{\phi_B}$ is defined as the ratio of electric flux to magnetic flux. The dimensions of $\eta$ are the same as that of:
questions.solution:
Electric Flux $\phi_E = \vec{E} \cdot \vec{A}$. Dimensions: $[\phi_E] = [E] \, [L^2] = [MLT^{-3}A^{-1}] \, [L^2] = [ML^3T^{-3}A^{-1}]$. Magnetic Flux $\phi_B = \vec{B} \cdot \vec{A}$. Dimensions: $[\phi_B] = [B] \, [L^2] = [MT^{-2}A^{-1}] \, [L^2] = [ML^2T^{-2}A^{-1}]$. The ratio is:
$?[\eta] = \left[ \frac{\phi_E}{\phi_B} \right] = \frac{[ML^3T^{-3}A^{-1}]}{[ML^2T^{-2}A^{-1}]} = [LT^{-1}]$
This is the dimension of velocity.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The ratio of the dimensions of Planck's constant ($h$) to that of the moment of inertia ($I$) is the same as the dimension of:
questions.solution:
Planck's constant ($h$) has dimensions of angular momentum. From $E = h\nu$,
$[h] = [E]/[\nu] = [ML^2T^{-2}] \big/ [T^{-1}] = [ML^2T^{-1}]$. Moment of Inertia $(I)$ has dimensions $[ML^2]$. The ratio is:
$\left[ \frac{h}{I} \right] = \frac{[ML^2T^{-1}]}{[ML^2]} = [T^{-1}]$
This is the dimension of frequency.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer.

List - I (Physical Quantity)List - II(Dimensional Formula)
(A) Poynting Vector(I) $[M^{-1}LT^2]$
(B) Compressibility(II) $[ML^2T^{-3}A^{-1}]$
(C) Voltage(III) $[J]$ (candela)
(D) Luminous Intensity(IV) $[MT^{-3}]$
questions.solution:
- (A) Poynting Vector $(\vec{S})$ represents energy flux density (Power/Area). $[\vec{S}] = \frac{[ML^2T^{-3}]}{[L^2]} = [MT^{-3}]$. So, A matches with IV.
- (B) Compressibility $(K)$ is the reciprocal of the Bulk Modulus $(B)$. $[B] = [\text{Pressure}] = [ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$. So,
$[K] = \frac{1}{[B]} = [M^{-1}LT^2]$. So, B matches with I.
- (C) Voltage $(V)$ : From $W = qV$, $[V] = \frac{[W]}{[q]} = \frac{[ML^2T^{-2}]}{[AT]} = [ML^2T^{-3}A^{-1}]$. So, C matches with II.
- (D) Luminous Intensity is a base quantity with the dimension of $[J]$ and unit Candela. So, D matches with III.
The correct matching is A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: If Planck's constant ($h$), the speed of light in vacuum ($c$) and Newton's gravitational constant ($G$) are taken as fundamental constants, then the dimensions of length (Planck Length) are proportional to:
questions.solution:
Let Length $L \propto h^a G^b c^d$. Writing the dimensions:
$[L^1] = [ML^2T^{-1}]^a [M^{-1}L^3T^{-2}]^b [LT^{-1}]^d [M^0L^1T^0] = [M^{a-b}L^{2a+3b+d}T^{-a-2b-d}]$ Equating the powers:
- M: $a - b = 0 \implies a = b$.
- T: $-a - 2b - d = 0 \implies -a - 2a - d = 0 \implies d = -3a$.
- L: $2a + 3b + d = 1 \implies 2a + 3a - 3a = 1 \implies 2a = 1 \implies a = 1/2$.
So, $a = 1/2, b = 1/2$, and $d = -3/2$. The relation is $L \propto h^{1/2} G^{1/2} c^{-3/2} \propto \sqrt{\frac{hG}{c^3}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The pair of physical quantities having the same dimensional formula is:
questions.solution:
Let's find the dimensions of each quantity in the options.
- Impulse: $[J] = [F \cdot t] = [MLT^{-2}] [T] = [MLT^{-1}]$. Surface Tension: $[S] = [F/L] = [MLT^{-2}] / [L] = [MT^{-2}]$. Not same.
- Angular Momentum: $[L] = [I\omega] = [ML^2] [T^{-1}] = [ML^2T^{-1}]$. Work: $[W] = [F \cdot d] = [MLT^{-2}] [L] = [ML^2T^{-2}]$. Not same.
- Work: $[W] = [ML^2T^{-2}]$. Torque: $[\tau] = [r \times F] = [L] [MLT^{-2}] = [ML^2T^{-2}]$. Same dimensions.
- Young's Modulus: $[Y] = [\text{Stress / Strain}] = [F/A] = [ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$. Energy: $[E] = [ML^2T^{-2}]$. Not same.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In Bernoulli's equation $P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + h\rho g = \text{constant}$, the dimensional formula of the constant is the same as that of:
questions.solution:
According to the principle of homogeneity, all terms in the equation must have the same dimensions. Let's find the dimension of the first term, Pressure (P). $[P] = \frac{[F]}{[A]} = \frac{[MLT^{-2}]}{[L^2]} = [ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$. Therefore, the constant on the right side must also have the dimension $[ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$. Now let's check the options
- Surface Tension: $[F/L] = [MT^{-2}]$.
- Energy Density: $\frac{[\text{Energy}]}{[\text{Volume}]} = \frac{[ML^2T^{-2}]}{[L^3]} = [ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$. This matches.
- Angular Momentum: $[ML^2T^{-1}].$
- Latent Heat: $[\text{Energy / Mass}]= \frac{[ML^2T^{-2}]}{[M]} = [L^2T^{-2}].$
The dimension of the constant matches that of Energy Density.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: If pressure $P$, velocity $V$ and time $T$ are taken as fundamental physical quantities, the dimensional formula of force is:
questions.solution:
Let the dimensional formula of force be $[F] = [P^a V^b T^c]$. Substituting the MLT dimensions:
$[MLT^{-2}] = [ML^{-1}T^{-2}]^a [LT^{-1}]^b [T]^c [M^1 L^1 T^{-2}] = [M^a L^{-a+b} T^{-2a-b+c}]$ Equating the exponents for each
fundamental dimension:
- M: $a = 1$
- L: $-a + b = 1 \implies -1 + b = 1 \implies b = 2$
- T: $-2a - b + c = -2 \implies -2(1) - 2 + c = -2 \implies -4 + c = -2 \implies c = 2$
Thus, the dimensional formula of force is $[PV^2T^2]$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The time period $T$ of a small liquid drop under surface tension $S$ depends on the density $\rho$, radius $r$, and surface tension $S$. If $T \propto S^a \rho^b r^c$, the values of $a, b, c$ are respectively:
questions.solution:
We are given $T = kS^a \rho^b r^c$. Writing dimensions on both sides:
$[T^1] = [MT^{-2}]^a [ML^{-3}]^b [L]^c [M^0L^0T^1] = [M^{a+b} L^{-3b+c} T^{-2a}]$ Equating the exponents:
- T: $-2a = 1 \implies a = -1/2.$
- M: $a + b = 0 \implies -1/2 + b = 0 \implies b = 1/2.$
- L: $-3b + c = 0 \implies -3(1/2) + c = 0 \implies c = 3/2.$
So, the values are $a = -1/2, b = 1/2, c = 3/2.$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The dimensions of gravitational constant $G$ are $[M^a L^b T^c]$. The values of $a, b,$ and $c$ are:
questions.solution:
From Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation, $F = G\frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$. So, $G = \frac{Fr^2}{m_1 m_2}$. Writing the dimensions:
$[G] = \frac{[MLT^{-2}] [L^2]}{[M][M]} = [M^{-1}L^3T^{-2}]$. Comparing with $[M^a L^b T^c]$, we get $a = -1, b = 3, c = -2.$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer.

List IList II
(A) Gas Constant (R)(I) $[L^2 T^{-2} K^{-1}]$
(B) Wien's Constant (b)(II) $[MT^{-3}]$
(C) Wave Intensity(III) $[LK]$
(D) Specific Heat Capacity(IV) $[ML^2 T^{-2} K^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}]$
questions.solution:
- (A) Gas Constant (R): From $PV = nRT, [R] = \frac{[P][V]}{[n][T]} = \frac{[ML^{-1}T^{-2}][L^3]}{[mol][K]} = [ML^2T^{-2}K^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}]$. So, A matches with IV.
- (B) Wien's Constant (b): From $\lambda_m T = b, [b] = [L][K]$. So, B matches with III.
- (C) Wave Intensity (I): Power per unit area. $[I] = \frac{[\text{Power}]}{[\text{Area}]} = \frac{[ML^2T^{-3}]}{[L^2]} = [MT^{-3}]$. So, C matches with II.
- (D) Specific Heat Capacity (s): From $Q = ms\Delta T, [s] = \frac{[Q]}{[m][\Delta T]} = \frac{[ML^2T^{-2}]}{[M][K]} = [L^2T^{-2}K^{-1}]$. So, D matches with I.
The correct matching is A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The dimensions of the ratio of angular momentum to linear momentum is the same as that of:
questions.solution:
The dimensional formula for angular momentum is $[L] = [I\omega] = [ML^2] [T^{-1}] = [ML^2T^{-1}]$. The dimensional formula for linear momentum is $[p] = [mv] = [M] [LT^{-1}] = [MLT^{-1}]$. The dimensions of their ratio are:
$$\left[ \frac{\text{Angular Momentum}}{\text{Linear Momentum}} \right] = \frac{[ML^2T^{-1}]}{[MLT^{-1}]} = [L]$$
This is the dimension of length.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: If force ( $F$ ), length ( $L$ ) and time ( $T$ ) are chosen as the fundamental quantities, then the dimensions of mass are:
questions.solution:
We know the dimensional formula for force is $[F] = [MLT^{-2}]$. We need to express mass (M) in terms of F, L, and T. From the formula, we can write:
$[M] = \frac{[F]}{[LT^{-2}]} = [FL^{-1}T^2]$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The dimensions of $\frac{1}{2} \epsilon_0 E^2$ ($\epsilon_0$: permittivity of free space; $E$: electric field) is:
questions.solution:
The quantity $\frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0 E^2$ represents the energy density of the electric field. Energy density is energy per unit volume. Dimension of Energy is $[ML^2T^{-2}]$. Dimension of Volume is $[L^3]$. Dimension of Energy Density
$= \frac{[\text{Energy}]}{[\text{Volume}]} = \frac{[ML^2T^{-2}]}{[L^3]} = [ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$. This is also the dimension of pressure.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
Which of the following equations is dimensionally correct?
( $q = \text{charge}, B = \text{magnetic field}, m = \text{mass}, v = \text{velocity}, r = \text{radius}$ )
questions.solution:
The magnetic force provides the centripetal force for a charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field:
$F_{magnetic} = F_{centripetal} \implies qvB = \frac{mv^2}{r}$. Solving for $r$ gives $r = \frac{mv}{qB}$. Let's check the dimensions of this correct physical equation. $[r] = [L]$. Dimensions of the right side:
$$\left[\frac{mv}{qB}\right] = \frac{[M][LT^{-1}]}{[AT][MT^{-2}A^{-1}]} = \frac{[MLT^{-1}]}{[MT^{-1}]} = [L]$$
The dimensions match, so the equation is dimensionally correct. The other options can be shown to be incorrect dimensionally. For example, option (a):
$$\left[\frac{mv^2}{qB}\right] = \left[\frac{mv}{qB}\right] \cdot [v] = [L][LT^{-1}] = [L^2T^{-1}] \neq [L]$$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The potential energy of a particle varies with position $x$ according to the relation $U(x) = \frac{A \sqrt{x}}{x+B}$. The dimensions of $AB$ are:
questions.solution:
From the principle of homogeneity:
- In the denominator $(x + B)$, the dimension of $B$ must be the same as the dimension of $x$. So, $[B] = [L]$.
- The dimension of $U(x)$ is potential energy, which is $[ML^2T^{-2}]$.
- The dimension of the entire expression $\frac{A\sqrt{x}}{x+B}$ must be that of energy.
$$\left[ \frac{A\sqrt{x}}{x+B} \right] = [ML^2T^{-2}]$$
$$\frac{[A][L^{1/2}]}{[L]} = [ML^2T^{-2}]$$
$$[A][L^{-1/2}] = [ML^2T^{-2}]$$
$[A] = [ML^{2.5}T^{-2}] = [ML^{5/2}T^{-2}]$
Now, the dimensions of the product $AB$:
$[AB] = [ML^{5/2}T^{-2}] \cdot [L] = [ML^{7/2}T^{-2}]$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The dimensions of the ratio of magnetic flux ( $\phi_B$ ) and electric flux ( $\phi_E$ ) is:
questions.solution:
Magnetic Flux $[\phi_B] = [B\cdot Area] = [MT^{-2}A^{-1}] \cdot [L^2] = [ML^2T^{-2}A^{-1}]$. Electric Flux $[\phi_E] = [E\cdot Area
] = [MLT^{-3}A^{-1}] \cdot [L^2] = [ML^3T^{-3}A^{-1}]$. The ratio is:
$$\left[\frac{\phi_B}{\phi_E}\right] = \frac{[ML^2T^{-2}A^{-1}]}{[ML^3T^{-3}A^{-1}]} = [L^{-1}T]$$
This is the reciprocal of velocity.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In the equation $(P + \frac{a}{V^2}) (V - b) = \text{constant}$, the units of $a$ are:
questions.solution:
From the principle of homogeneity, the term $\frac{a}{V^2}$ must have the same units as pressure $P$. So, unit of $a = (\text{unit of } P) \times (\text{unit of } V^2)$. In the CGS system, the unit of pressure is $\text{dyne/cm}^2$ and the unit of volume is $\text{cm}^3$. Unit of $a = (\text{ dyne
/cm}^2) \times (\text{cm}^3)^2 = (\text{ dyne /cm}^2) \times (\text{cm}^6) = \text{dyne} \cdot \text{cm}^4$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The escape velocity $v_e$ from a planet depends on the universal gravitational constant $G$, the mass of the planet $M$, and its radius $R$ as $v_e = kG^a M^b R^c$, where $k$ is a dimensionless constant. The value of $2(a + b + c)$ is ________.
questions.solution:
The dimensional equation is $[v_e] = [G]^a[M]^b[R]^c$. Substituting the dimensions of each quantity:
$[LT^{-1}] = [M^{-1}L^3T^{-2}]^a [M]^b [L]^c [M^0L^1T^{-1}] = [M^{-a+b}L^{3a+c}T^{-2a}]$ Equating the exponents for M, L, and T:
- For T: $-2a = -1 \implies a = 1/2$.
- For M: $-a + b = 0 \implies b = a = 1/2$.
- For L: $3a + c = 1 \implies 3(1/2) + c = 1 \implies c = 1 - 3/2 = -1/2$.
The required value is $2(a + b + c) = 2(1/2 + 1/2 - 1/2) = 2(1/2) = 1$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In a thermodynamic process, the pressure $P$ of a gas is related to its volume $V$ as $P = \frac{\alpha - t^2}{\beta V}$, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants and $t$ is time. The dimensions of $\alpha / \beta$ are given by $[M^x L^y T^z]$. The value of $x + y + z$ is ________.
questions.solution:
From the principle of homogeneity, in the numerator $(\alpha - t^2)$, the dimensions of $\alpha$ must be the same as the dimensions of $t^2$. So, $[\alpha] = [t^2] = [T^2]$. Now, considering the entire equation: $[P] = \frac{[\alpha]}{[\beta][V]}$ We can find the dimensions of
$\beta : [\beta] = \frac{[\alpha]}{[P][V]} = \frac{[T^2]}{[ML^{-1}T^{-2}][L^3]} = \frac{[T^2]}{[ML^2T^{-2}]} = [M^{-1}L^{-2}T^4]$. Now, we find the dimensions of the ratio $\alpha/\beta :$
$$\left[\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\right] = \frac{[T^2]}{[M^{-1}L^{-2}T^4]} = [ML^2T^{-2}]$$
Comparing this with $[M^xL^yT^z]$, we have $x = 1, y = 2, z = -2$. The required value is $x + y + z = 1 + 2 + (-2) = 1$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The velocity $v$ of water waves may depend on their wavelength $\lambda$, the density of water $\rho$, and the acceleration due to gravity $g$. It is found that $v = k\lambda^a \rho^b g^c$. The value of $2(a + c)$ is ________.
questions.solution:
The relation is $v = k\lambda^a\rho^bg^c$. Writing the dimensions: $[v] = [LT^{-1}] [\lambda] = [L] [\rho] = [ML^{-3}] [g] = [LT^{-2}]$ Substituting into the equation: $[LT^{-1}] = [L]^a [ML^{-3}]^b [LT^{-2}]^c [M^0L^1T^{-1}] = [M^bL^{a-3b+c}T^{-2c}]$ Equating powers:
- For M: $b = 0$.
- For T: $-2c = -1 \implies c = 1/2$.
- For L: $a - 3b + c = 1 \implies a - 3(0) + 1/2 = 1 \implies a = 1/2$.
So, $a = 1/2, b = 0, c = 1/2$. The value of $2(a + c) = 2(1/2 + 1/2) = 2(1) = 2$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The position of a particle is given by $x = A \sin(\omega t) + Bt^2 + Ct \cos(\omega t)$. If the dimensions of $A, B$ and $C$ are $[L^p T^q]$, $[L^r T^s]$ and $[L^u T^v]$ respectively, then the value of $p + q + r + s + u + v$ is ________.
questions.solution:
From the principle of homogeneity, each term on the right side must have the dimension of position, $[L]$.
- For the term $A \sin(\omega t) :$ The argument of sine must be dimensionless, so $[\omega t] = 1 \Longrightarrow [\omega] = [T^{-1}]$. The term $A$ must have the dimension of position. So, $[A] = [L] = [L^1 T^0]$. This gives $p = 1, q = 0$.
- For the term $B t^2 : [B] [t^2] = [L] \Longrightarrow [B] [T^2] = [L] \Longrightarrow [B] = [L T^{-2}] = [L^1 T^{-2}]$. This gives $r = 1, s = -2$.
- For the term $Ct \cos(\omega t) :$ The argument of cosine is dimensionless. The term Ct must have the dimension of position. So, $[C][t] = [L] \Longrightarrow [C][T] = [L] \Longrightarrow [C] = [L T^{-1}] = [L^1 T^{-1}]$. This gives $u = 1, v = -1$.
The required sum is $p + q + r + s + u + v = 1 + 0 + 1 + (-2) + 1 + (-1) = 1 + 1 - 2 + 1 - 1 = 0$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A quantity $\alpha$ is given by $\alpha = \frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 hc}$, where $e$ is the electric charge, $\epsilon_0$ is the permittivity of free space, $h$ is Planck's constant and $c$ is the speed of light. If the dimensional formula of $\alpha$ is expressed as $[M^p L^q T^r]$, the value of $p^2 + q^2 + r^2$ is_______.
questions.solution: The problem states that the quantity $\alpha$ (the fine-structure constant) is dimensionless. A dimensionless quantity has no dependence on the fundamental dimensions of mass (M), length (L), and time (T). This means that the dimensional formula is $[M^0 L^0 T^0]$. By comparing this with the given formula $[M^p L^q T^r]$, we can equate the exponents: $p = 0q = 0r = 0$ The required value is $p^2 + q^2 + r^2 = 0^2 + 0^2 + 0^2 = 0$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.text: If $z = x + iy, x \neq 0$, satisfies the equation $z^2 = i|z|^2$, then $z$ lies on:
questions.solution:
Given $z^2 = i|z|^2$.
Let $z = x + iy$.
$(x + iy)^2 = i(x^2 + y^2) \implies x^2 - y^2 + 2ixy = i(x^2 + y^2)$.
Equating real and imaginary parts:
1) $x^2 - y^2 = 0 \implies y = \pm x$.
2) $2xy = x^2 + y^2$.
If $y = x$ (and $x \neq 0$), then $2x^2 = x^2 + x^2$, which is true.
If $y = -x$ (and $x \neq 0$), then $-2x^2 = x^2 + (-x)^2 = 2x^2 \implies 4x^2 = 0 \implies x = 0$, a contradiction.
Thus, $z$ lies on the line $y = x$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.text: If $z_1, z_2$ are complex numbers such that $\overline{z_1} + i\overline{z_2} = 0$ and $\arg(z_1 z_2) = \pi$, then $\arg(z_1)$ equals:
questions.solution:
$\overline{z_1} = -i\overline{z_2}$.
Taking conjugates, $z_1 = iz_2$.
Let $\arg(z_1) = \theta_1$ and $\arg(z_2) = \theta_2$.
From $z_1 = iz_2$, we have $\arg(z_1) = \arg(i) + \arg(z_2)$, so $\theta_1 = \pi / 2 + \theta_2$.
Given $\arg(z_1 z_2) = \pi$, we have $\theta_1 + \theta_2 = \pi$.
Substituting $\theta_2 = \pi - \theta_1$ into the first equation:
$\theta_1 = \pi / 2 + (\pi - \theta_1) \implies 2\theta_1 = 3\pi / 2 \implies \theta_1 = 3\pi / 4$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.text: The area (in sq. units) of the region $\{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z - 1| \le 1, Re(z) \ge 1, Im(z) \ge 0\}$ is:
questions.solution:
$|z - 1| \le 1$ is a circle centered at $(1, 0)$ with radius $1$.
$Re(z) \ge 1$ is the region to the right of a line parallel to the y-axis passing through the center.
$Im(z) \ge 0$ is the upper half-plane.
The intersection of these three regions is the quarter of the circle that lies in the first quadrant.
Area $= \frac{1}{4} \pi r^2 = \frac{1}{4} (1)^2 = \pi / 4$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.text: Let $|z_1 - 10| \le 3$ and $|z_2| \le 5$. Then the minimum value of $|z_1 - z_2|$ is:
questions.solution:
$z_1$ lies in a circle with center $C_1 (10, 0)$ and radius $r_1 = 3$.
$z_2$ lies in a circle with center $C_2 (0, 0)$ and radius $r_2 = 5$.
The distance between centers is $d = 10$. Since $d > r_1 + r_2$ ($10 > 8$), the circles are separate.
The minimum distance is $d - r_1 - r_2 = 10 - 3 - 5 = 2$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.text: If $z_1, z_2, z_3$ are the vertices of an equilateral triangle and $z_0$ is its orthocenter, then $z_1^2 + z_2^2 + z_3^2$ equals:
questions.solution:
For an equilateral triangle, the orthocenter and centroid are the same, so $z_0 = (z_1 + z_2 + z_3) / 3$.
A key property is $z_1^2 + z_2^2 + z_3^2 = z_1 z_2 + z_2 z_3 + z_3 z_1$.
Also, $(z_1 + z_2 + z_3)^2 = \sum z_1^2 + 2 \sum z_1 z_2$. This gives $(3 z_0)^2 = \sum z_1^2 + 2 \sum z_1^2 = 3 \sum z_1^2$.
Thus, $z_1^2 + z_2^2 + z_3^2 = 3 z_0^2$.

The conjugate of $-6 - 24i$ is $-6 + 24i$.
$(x - iy)(3 + 5i) = (3x + 5y) + i(5x - 3y)$.
Equating this to $-6 + 24i$: $3x + 5y = -6$ and $5x - 3y = 24$.
Solving these simultaneous equations gives $x = 3$ and $y = -3$.

questions.text: The maximum value of $|z|$ when the complex number $z$ satisfies $\left|z - \frac{4}{z}\right| = 2$ is:
questions.solution:
By the triangle inequality, $|z| = |(z - \frac{4}{z}) + \frac{4}{z}| \le |z - \frac{4}{z}| + |\frac{4}{z}|$.
Let $|z| = r$. Then $r \le 2 + \frac{4}{r}$.
$r^2 \le 2r + 4 \implies r^2 - 2r - 4 \le 0$. The roots of $r^2 - 2r - 4 = 0$ are $1 \pm \sqrt{5}$.
So, $1 - \sqrt{5} \le r \le 1 + \sqrt{5}$. Since $r \ge 0$, we have $0 \le r \le 1 + \sqrt{5}$.
The maximum value of $|z|$ is $1 + \sqrt{5}$.

questions.solution:
Suppose $z = \frac{3 + 2i\sin\theta}{1 - 2i\sin\theta}$
since, $z$ is purely imaginary, then $z + \bar{z} = 0$
$\implies \frac{3 + 2i\sin\theta}{1 - 2i\sin\theta} + \frac{3 - 2i\sin\theta}{1 + 2i\sin\theta} = 0$
$\implies \frac{(3 + 2i\sin\theta)(1 + 2i\sin\theta) + (3 - 2i\sin\theta)(1 - 2i\sin\theta)}{1 + 4\sin^2\theta} = 0$

questions.text: The set of all $\alpha \in R$, for which $w = \frac{1+(1-8\alpha)z}{1-z}$ is a purely imaginary number, for all $z \in C$ satisfying $|z| = 1$ and $Re(z) \neq 1$, is:
questions.solution:
It is given that $|z| = 1 \& \text{Re}(z) \neq 1$
Lets assume $z = x + iy \Rightarrow x^2 + y^2 = 1 \dots (1)$
Also,
$$w = \frac{1 + (1 - 8\alpha)z}{1 - z}$$
$$\Rightarrow w = \frac{1 + (1 - 8\alpha)(x + iy)}{1 - (x + iy)}$$
Multiply and divide above equation by $(1 - x) + iy$, we get
$$w = \frac{(1 + (1 - 8\alpha)(x + iy))((1 - x) + iy)}{(1 - (x + iy))((1 - x) + iy)}$$
Solving it, we get
$$w = \frac{[1 + x(1 - 8\alpha)](1 - x) - (1 - 8\alpha)y^2}{(1 - x)^2 + y^2} + i \frac{[1 + x(1 - 8\alpha)]y - (1 - 8\alpha)y(1 - x)}{(1 - x)^2 + y^2}$$
It is also given that, $w$ is purely imaginary. Therefore, $\text{Re}(w) = 0$
$$\text{Re}(w) = \frac{[1 + x(1 - 8\alpha)](1 - x) - (1 - 8\alpha)y^2}{(1 - x)^2 + y^2} = 0$$
$$\Rightarrow (1 - x) + x(1 - 8\alpha)(1 - x) = (1 - 8\alpha)y^2$$
$$\Rightarrow (1 - x) + x(1 - 8\alpha) - x^2(1 - 8\alpha) = (1 - 8\alpha)y^2$$
$$\Rightarrow (1 - x) + x(1 - 8\alpha) = 1 - 8\alpha \dots [\because x^2 + y^2 = 1]$$
$$\Rightarrow 1 - 8\alpha = 1$$
$$\Rightarrow \alpha = 0$$
$$\therefore \alpha \in \{0\}}$$

In an experiment $0.25\text{ mol}$ of $\text{NH}_3$ is formed when $0.5\text{ mol}$ of $\text{N}_2$ is reacted with $0.5\text{ mol}$ of $\text{H}_2$. What is $\%$ yield ?
questions.solution:
Consider the reaction, $\text{N}_2 + 3\text{H}_2 \rightarrow \text{NH}_3$
From the reaction,
$1$ mole of $\text{N}_2$ reacts with $3$ moles of $\text{H}_2$
$0.5$ mole of $\text{N}_2$ will react with $3 \times 0.5$ i.e. $1.5$ moles of $\text{H}_2$
$\therefore$ Moles given of $\text{H}_2$ i.e. $0.5$ is less than the required i.e. $1.5$
$\therefore \text{H}_2$ is limiting reagent
From the reaction,
$3$ moles of $\text{H}_2$ forms $2$ moles of $\text{NH}_3$
$\therefore 0.5$ moles of $\text{H}_2$ will form $\frac{2 \times 0.5}{3}$ i.e. $0.33$ moles of $\text{NH}_3$
$\therefore$ The expected moles of $\text{NH}_3 = 0.33$
But, the actual moles of $\text{NH}_3 = 0.25$
$\therefore \% \text{ yield } \frac{0.25}{0.33} \times 100 = 75.75\%$
The correct option is (a).

$\text{Mass} = \frac{56 \times 2 \times 342}{22.4 \times 11} = 155.5\text{ g}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text:
How many kilograms (approximately) of pure $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ could be obtained from $1\text{ kg}$ of Iron pyrites ($\text{FeS}_2$) according to the following reactions?
(Atomic mass of Fe-56, S-32, O-16, H-1)
$4\text{FeS}_2 + 11\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 + 8\text{SO}_2$
$2\text{SO}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{SO}_3$
$\text{SO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$
questions.solution:
$4\text{FeS}_2 + 15\text{O}_2 + 8\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 + 8\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$
$4 \times 120\text{g}$ of $\text{FeS}_2$ yield $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 = 8 \times 98\text{ g}$
$1000\text{ g}$ of $\text{FeS}_2$ will yield $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 = \frac{8 \times 98}{4 \times 120} \times 1000$
$= 1.63\text{ kg}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: $2.4\text{ kg}$ of carbon is made to react with $1.35\text{ kg}$ of Aluminium to form $\text{Al}_4\text{C}_3$. The maximum amount in kg of Aluminium carbide formed is (Atomic mass $\text{Al} = 27$)
questions.solution:
$\begin{array}{lcccc} & 4\text{ Al} & + & 3\text{ C} & \rightarrow & \text{Al}_4\text{C}_3 \\ \text{W:} & 1350\text{g} & & 2400\text{g} & \\ \text{n:} & 50 & & 200 & \\ \text{no.:} & 50/4(\text{LR}) & & 200/3 & \end{array}$
Moles of $\text{Al}_4\text{C}_3 = \text{moles of Al}/4 = 12.5$
Hence, weight of $\text{Al}_4\text{C}_3 = \text{moles} \times \text{Molar mass of } \text{Al}_4\text{C}_3 = 12.5 \times 144 = 1800\text{g}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: For the reaction $3\text{A} + 4\text{B} \rightarrow 5\text{C} + 2\text{D}$, $6$ moles of A and $10$ moles of B will produce
questions.solution:
$\begin{array}{lcccc} & 3\text{ A} & + & 4\text{ B} & \rightarrow 5\text{ C} + 2\text{ D} \\ \text{n:} & 6 & & 10 & \\ \text{no.:} & 6/3(\text{LR}) & & 10/4 & \end{array}$
$\text{n}_{\text{c}} = 6/3 \times 5 = 10 \ \& \ \text{n}_{\text{D}} = 6/3 \times 2 = 4$
10 moles of C and 4 moles of D will be produced.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: $10\text{ moles N}_2$ and $15\text{ moles of H}_2$ were allowed to react over a suitable catalyst. $10\text{ moles of NH}_3$ were formed. The remaining moles of $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{H}_2$ respectively are:
questions.solution:
$\begin{array}{lcccc} & \text{N}_2 & + & 3\text{ H}_2 & \rightarrow 2\text{ NH}_3 \\ \text{t}=0 & 10 & & 15 & - \\ \text{t}=\text{t} & 10-\text{x} & & 15-3\text{x} & 2\text{x} \end{array}$
Here, $2\text{x} = 10 \Rightarrow \text{x} = 5$
hence, remaining moles of $\text{N}_2 = 5 \ \& \ \text{H}_2 = 0$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: $12\text{ g}$ of $\text{Mg}$ (atomic mass $= 24$) on reacting completely with hydrochloric acid gives hydrogen gas, the volume of which at STP would be
questions.solution:
$\text{Mg} + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_2 + \text{H}_2$
$\because 24\text{g Mg evolves } 22.4\text{L } \text{H}_2 \text{ at STP}$
$\therefore 12\text{g Mg will evolve } \text{H}_2 \text{ at STP} = \frac{22.4}{24} \times 12 = 11.2\text{L at STP}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text:
For the following reaction the mass of $\text{CO}_2$ produced from $445\text{ g}$ of $\text{C}_{57}\text{H}_{110}\text{O}_6$ is:
$2\text{C}_{57}\text{H}_{110}\text{O}_6(\text{s}) + 163\text{ O}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow 114\text{CO}_2(\text{g}) + 110\text{ H}_2\text{O}(\text{l})$
questions.solution:
For the given reaction:
$2\text{C}_{57}\text{H}_{110}\text{O}_6(s) + 163\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 114\text{CO}_2(g) + 110\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$
$n_{\text{C}_{57}\text{H}_{110}\text{O}_6} = \frac{445}{890} = 0.5$
Now, moles of Carbon dioxide = $\frac{114}{2} \times 0.5 = 28.5$
$\therefore$ Mass of Carbon dioxide = $28.5 \times 44 = 1254\text{g}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: In a reaction, $10\text{g}$ of calcium reacts with $17.8\text{g}$ of chlorine to form calcium chloride. What is the mass of calcium chloride formed?
questions.solution:
According to the Law of Conservation of Mass, the mass of the products is equal to the mass of the reactants. Therefore,
$10\text{g} + 17.8\text{g} = 27.8\text{g}$ of calcium chloride is formed.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text:
A sample of $0.5\text{ g}$ of a metal M reacts completely with dilute hydrochloric acid, producing $240\text{ mL}$ of hydrogen gas at STP. Find the molar mass of the metal M, assuming it forms a divalent cation $M^{+2}$ in the reaction:

$M + 2HCl \rightarrow MCl_2 + H_2$

(Given: $1\text{ mol of gas at STP} = 22.4\text{ L}$)
questions.solution:
The volume of hydrogen gas produced is $240\text{ mL} = 0.240\text{ L}$.
At STP, 1 mole of any gas occupies $22.4\text{ L}$.
Moles of $H_2 = \frac{0.240\text{ L}}{22.4\text{ L mol}^{-1}} = 0.0107\text{ mol}$
Balanced equation: $M + 2HCl \rightarrow \text{MCl}_2 + H_2$
$1\text{ mol of } M \rightarrow 1\text{ mol of } H_2$
$\therefore$ Moles of metal $M = 0.0107\text{ mol}$
Given mass of metal $M = 0.5\text{ g}$
Molar mass of $M = \frac{\text{Mass of metal}}{\text{Moles of metal}} = \frac{0.5\text{ g}}{0.0107\text{ mol}} \approx 46.7\text{ g mol}^{-1}$
Answer: The molar mass of the metal $M$ is approximately $46.7\text{ gmol}^{-1}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text:
$3.0\text{ g}$ an impure sample of sodium sulphate dissolved in water was treated with an excess of barium chloride solution when $1.74\text{ g}$ of $\text{BaSO}_4$ were obtained as a dry precipitate. Calculate the percentage purity of the sample.
(Round off the answer to the whole number)
questions.solution:
$\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{BaCl}_2 \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4 + 2\text{NaCl}$
$142\text{ g} \qquad \qquad \quad 233\text{ g}$
$233\text{ g of } \text{BaSO}_4 \text{ are produced from } 142\text{ g of } \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$
$\therefore 1.74\text{ g of } \text{BaSO}_4 \text{ would be produced by} = \frac{142}{233} \times 1.74 = 1.06\text{ g of } \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$
$\% \text{ purity of } \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 = \frac{1.06}{3.0} \times 100 = 35.33\%$
Rounding off to the whole number, as the question asks: $\% \text{ purity} \approx 35\%$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text:
A particular $100$-octane aviation gasoline used $1.00\text{ cm}^3$ of tetraethyl lead $(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_4\text{ Pb}$ of density $1.66\text{ g/cc}$, per litre of product. This compound is made as follows
$4\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl} + 4\text{NaPb} \rightarrow (\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_4\text{ Pb} + 4\text{NaCl} + 3\text{Pb}$. How many gram of ethyl chloride is needed to make enough tetraethyl lead for $1\text{L}$ of gasoline? (mol. wt of $(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_4\text{ Pb}$ is $323\text{ g/mol}$) (Report the answer to nearest integer)
questions.solution:
"THIS IS A HIGH WEIGHTAGE TOPIC"

The mass of $1\text{cc}$ of $(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_4\text{ Pb}$ is $1 \times 1.66 = 1.66\text{ g}$ and this is the amount needed per litre. No. of moles of $(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_4\text{ Pb}$ needed = $\frac{1.66}{323} = 0.00514$
$1\text{ mole of } (\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_4\text{ Pb requires}$
$4 \times (0.00514) = 0.0206\text{ moles of } \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$
$\therefore \text{ Mass of } \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl} = 0.0206 \times 64.5 = 1.33\text{g}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text:
In the preparation of iron from haematite ($\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$) by the reduction with carbon
$\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 + \text{C} \rightarrow \text{Fe} + \text{CO}_2$
How much $80\text{uch}$ pure iron (in g) may be produced from $120\text{ kg}$ of $90\text{\%}$ pure $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$?

(At. mass Fe - 56, O - 16)
questions.solution:
Balanced reaction is
$2\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 + 3\text{C} \rightarrow 4\text{Fe} + 3\text{CO}_2$
Number of moles of $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$
$= \left(\frac{120 \times 1000}{2 \times 56 + 48}\right) \times \frac{90}{100}$
Mass of $80\%$ pure iron produced
$= \frac{120 \times 1000 \times 0.9}{2 \times 56 + 48} \times \frac{2 \times 56}{0.8}$
$= 94500\text{ gram}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text:
During the decomposition of potassium chlorate $\text{KClO}_3$ oxygen gas is released:

$2\text{KClO}_3 \rightarrow 2\text{KCl} + 3\text{O}_2$

If $245\text{ g}$ of potassium chlorate decomposes completely, calculate the mass of oxygen gas produced.
questions.solution:
Reaction: $2KClO_3 \rightarrow 2KCl + 3O_2$
Molar mass of $KClO_3 = 39.10 + 35.45 + 3 \times 16.00 = 122.55\text{ g mol}^{-1}$
Moles of potassium chlorate decomposed: $\frac{245\text{ g}}{122.55\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 2.00\text{ mol}$
Using stoichiometry: $2\text{ mol } KClO_3 \rightarrow 3\text{ mol } O_2$
$\therefore$ Moles of $O_2 = \frac{3}{2} \times 2.00 = 3.00\text{ mol}$
Mass of oxygen gas produced: $3.00\text{ mol} \times 32.00\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 96.0\text{ g}$
